title: Theoretical Models of Dyslexia
description: Several theoretical models have been proposed to explain dyslexia, each emphasizing different aspects of the disorder. These models help researchers and practitioners understand the underlying mechanisms and guide intervention approaches.

sections.name: Phonological Deficit Hypothesis
sections.description: The phonological deficit hypothesis proposes that the cognitive basis of many specific reading difficulties is a phonological deficit, characterized by difficulties in processing and manipulating the sound structure of words and grapheme-phoneme correspondences.
keyPoints: Difficulties processing and manipulating the sound structure of words
Difficulties with grapheme-phoneme (letter-sound) correspondences
Difficulties with rapid automatized naming (RAN)
Phonological deficits are evident across languages and orthographies
Phonological processing impairments predict reading difficulties
sections.evidence: For many years, dyslexia has mainly been explained within the context of the phonological theory, which postulates that dyslexic readers have difficulties with processing and manipulating the sound structure of words, grapheme-phoneme correspondences, and rapid automatized naming.

sources.title: The co-occurrence of neurodevelopmental problems in dyslexia

sections.name: Double-Deficit Hypothesis
sections.description: The double-deficit hypothesis (DDH) posits that difficulties in phonological awareness (PA) and rapid automatized naming (RAN) represent two distinct causes of reading disability, with slow RAN associated with slow reading, whereas poor PA is characterized by inaccurate reading and spelling.
keyPoints: Two distinct causes of reading disability: PA deficits and RAN deficits
Slow RAN associated with slow reading
Poor PA characterized by inaccurate reading and spelling
Distinct subtypes with single and double deficits
PA and RAN contribute independently to reading ability

subtypes.name: PA-disabled
subtypes.characteristics: Selective deficits in phonological and morphological awareness, intact RAN

subtypes.name: RAN-disabled
subtypes.characteristics: Impaired RAN but preserved phonological and morphological awareness

subtypes.name: Doubly-disabled
subtypes.characteristics: Deficits in both PA and RAN

sections.name: Temporal Sampling Theory
sections.description: Temporal Sampling theory proposes that infants and children extract a phonological system via automatic sensory-motor learning of a hierarchy of amplitude modulations nested in the amplitude envelope of the speech signal, and that impaired encoding of low-frequency envelope information (<10Hz, delta and theta band) underlies phonological deficits in dyslexia.
keyPoints: Phonological system extracted via automatic sensory-motor learning
Learning involves hierarchy of amplitude modulations in speech signal
Impaired encoding of low-frequency envelope information (<10Hz)
Delta and theta band information specifically affected
Explains phonological deficits at neural level
sections.mechanism: Infants and children extract a phonological system via automatic sensory-motor learning of a hierarchy of amplitude modulations nested in the amplitude envelope of the speech signal. In developmental dyslexia, encoding of low-frequency envelope information <10Hz (delta and theta band information) is impaired.

sections.name: Cerebellar Theory
sections.description: The cerebellar theory states, with mixed empirical support, that poor automaticity and motor deficits in individuals with dyslexia may be associated with a dysfunction of the cerebellum.
keyPoints: Poor automaticity may be associated with cerebellar dysfunction
Motor deficits in dyslexia may be linked to cerebellum
Evidence is mixed and controversial
Not widely accepted as primary explanation

sections.name: Multiple-Deficit Model
sections.description: Recent studies suggest that dyslexia typically occurs as a result of multiple deficits rather than a single phonological deficit, and some diagnosed cases show no phonological problems at all.
keyPoints: Dyslexia typically results from multiple deficits
Not all cases show phonological problems
Accounts for heterogeneity in dyslexia profiles
Explains co-occurrence with other disorders
Variable expression across individuals
advantages: Accounts for heterogeneity in dyslexia profiles
Explains co-occurrence with other neurodevelopmental disorders
Accounts for variable expression across individuals

developmentalTrajectories.title: Developmental Trajectory Models
developmentalTrajectories.description: Models that explain how dyslexia develops over time.

models.name: Rate-Disabled vs Accuracy-Disabled Subtypes
models.description: Longitudinal research supports the distinction between rate-disabled and accuracy-disabled subtypes of dyslexia, with preschool deficits in rapid automatized naming (RAN) predicting slow but accurate reading in first grade, and deficits in phonological and morphological awareness predicting both inaccurate and slow reading.
models.evidence: In first grade, the PA+MA-disabled group demonstrated significantly lower reading accuracy compared to both the RAN-only disabled and control groups. The RAN-only subgroup exhibited slow reading but intact accuracy.

models.name: Developmental Timing Framework
models.description: The developmental timing framework proposes that learning disabilities emerge from maturational asynchrony among interacting neural, cognitive, linguistic, sensorimotor, and executive systems rather than from isolated deficits within a single domain.
keyPoints: Learning disabilities emerge from maturational asynchrony
Involves multiple interacting systems
Not from isolated deficits in single domain
Explains heterogeneity and variable expression

sources.title: When development falls out of sync: A developmental timing framework for learning disabilities

computationalModels.description: Theoretical distinctions in how brain differences produce cognitive profiles.

domainRelevance.name: Domain-Relevant Accounts
domainRelevance.description: Widespread brain differences in processing properties differentially impact domains that rely particularly on those properties

domainSpecific.name: Domain-Specific Accounts
domainSpecific.description: Underactivation or structural differences in specific brain regions involved in phonological processing

comorbidityModels.title: Comorbidity Models
comorbidityModels.description: Models explaining why dyslexia frequently co-occurs with other disorders.

models.name: Additive Model of RD-ADHD Comorbidity
models.description: The additive model of RD-ADHD comorbidity posits that children with ADHD + RD exhibit more severe deficits in attention, inhibition, working memory, and RAN due to the combined impairments of both disorders, which is supported by additive effects in cognitive profiles.
models.evidence: Children with ADHD + RD exhibit more severe deficits in attention, inhibition, working memory, and RAN due to the combined impairments of both disorders.

models.name: ESSENCE Framework
models.description: The ESSENCE framework (Early Symptomatic Syndromes Eliciting Neurodevelopmental Clinical Examinations) covers different kinds of neurodevelopmental difficulties and disorders to draw attention to the early onset of symptoms and the universal co-existence among them, challenging compartmentalization into distinct diagnostic categories.
keyPoints: Covers different kinds of neurodevelopmental difficulties
Draws attention to early onset of symptoms
Universal co-existence among disorders
Challenges compartmentalization into distinct diagnostic categories

disclaimer: Theoretical models continue to evolve as research advances. No single model fully explains all aspects of dyslexia. The multiple-deficit model, integrating multiple cognitive risk factors, is gaining support. These models should guide research and intervention rather than serve as rigid diagnostic categories.
